source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Trained on the Same Data Learn Different Features

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Minor formatting artifacts flatten some mathematical superscripts and symbols.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports that independently initialized SAEs often learn different features despite using the same model and training data, refining and challenging claims of seed-invariant or universal features.
record.gate_note: The paper directly measures SAE feature matching and overlap across random seeds, and reports how overlap changes with SAE size, training settings, model positions, architectures, and similarity metrics. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs that differ only in random seed and measures how many dictionary features recur. This bears on V3 for SAE networks, and its overlap results argue that seed convergence is partial and plateaus (V7). One metric comparison bears narrowly on V6. Different underlying models are never compared, so V1, V2, V4 and V5 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SAEs differing only in seed learn different feature sets, so SAE features are a pragmatic decomposition rather than a universal list. Two qualifications: 'diverge with increasing scale' refers to SAE and model scale in seed overlap, not to cross-model convergence. They also attribute the result to the nonconvexity of the SAE loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests SAE feature overlap across random seeds, not similarity of representations between independently trained neural networks or models. It uses Hungarian matching and cosine similarity to compare feature vectors.
record.method_sensitivity: Overlap varies with SAE latent count, TopK k, training time, layer, model position, SAE architecture, and sparsity loss. Hungarian matching and maximum cosine similarity give similar results.

fits_no_version.finding: Seed overlap of SAE features decreases with SAE size, and is lower for the larger model (Llama 8B) at the same expansion factor. The authors say SAEs diverge with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-derived features become less seed-stable as dictionary size and model size grow.

record.problems: The main comparisons concern SAE features trained on the same underlying model and data, so they do not directly establish convergence or divergence of the underlying models' representations. Many setting-dependent trends are described qualitatively from figures without numeric values or stated uncertainty. The paper reports a 0.7 shared-feature threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying reported results were left out.

untested.parts: No comparison of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives or data, and no trend with model capability.
Features of the underlying LLMs across seeds are not tested; only SAE dictionaries trained on a fixed model are compared.
No linear maps, stitching, relative representations or unpaired mapping between models.
No recurrence of features across different models; all comparisons are within one model.
Input data, out-of-distribution inputs, neighbour counts and non-cosine measures are not varied; the threshold sweep (Fig. A1) is not quantified.
Whether shared data or objectives explain the alignment is not tested.

missing.what: Power law with an offset fits the orphan-fraction curve significantly better than one without, implying a floor of persistent orphans.
Fraction shared as a function of the cosine threshold; mean alignment 0.72 for matching indices vs 0.33 for differing indices.
Smaller models, and smaller SAEs on the same model, have higher fractions of shared features. Llama 8B overlap is much lower at the same expansion factor of 36.
Abstract states the result holds across two datasets and multiple layers of three LLMs; per-dataset results are not recorded.

record.verdict_notes: The 215 latent count is an extraction artifact for 2^15 (32K). The rows bear on seed convergence of SAE dictionaries, not of the underlying LLM representations, so they support V3 only by analogy. Hyperparameter rows were relinked from V6 to V3 because they vary the trained system, not the similarity measure.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether representations of independently trained foundation models with different architectures, objectives, or data become more aligned as model size or capability increases.
No paired image-caption data or vision-language alignment is tested.

Tests SAE features learned from different initializations, not the convergence of features or shared subspaces in the underlying language models themselves; it does not establish whether units or bases in those networks match.
Hungarian matching compares SAE feature vectors; the paper does not test mapping one model's representations onto another's, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mappings.
It evaluates SAE feature explanations and overlap across seeds for the same underlying model, not recurrence of the same interpretable features or circuits across different models.
Compares Hungarian matching with maximum cosine similarity and varies SAE settings. It does not vary the input data or test out-of-distribution inputs, and does not test neighbour-count choices.

Reports incomplete overlap and a slowly declining orphan-latent fraction across seeds, but does not test whether shared data or objectives cause alignment, or compare that explanation with a common model of reality.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Matched SAE features across two independently initialized seeds using Hungarian matching and the shared-latent threshold.

conditions.value: first 8B tokens of the Pile, same order for both SAEs
cosine similarity >= 0.7 for both encoder and decoder matchings

rows.measure: Fraction of SAE latents classified as shared across the two seeds
rows.note: The paper says the 42% result uses its shared-latent definition.
rows.check: For V3 the state is partial: 42% shared. For V7 the effect is observed: overlap is far from complete. The 32K latents appear as '215' because of a formatting loss (2^15).

source_check.correct: 32,768 (2^15) latents. Shared latents must have the same counterpart in encoder and decoder matchings, with cosine similarity >=0.7 in both. State: partial for V3; observed for V7.

source_check.problem: The latent count lost its exponent, the shared criterion omits counterpart agreement, and partial does not describe the observed V7 incompleteness.

rows.subject: Pythia 160M
rows.operation_detail: Related each latent's seed-matched cosine similarity to its firing frequency.

conditions.value: base SAE matched against 8 other seeds

rows.measure: Firing frequency by degree of sharing/alignment
rows.value: Latents that fire most frequently are shared with all eight other SAEs; those firing least frequently are not shared with any. Some orphan latents fire more often on average than latents shared with all SAEs.
rows.note: This reports frequency patterns, not only an overall overlap rate.
rows.check: This is a frequency pattern among shared and orphan latents. It does not show plateau or causes, so the V7 link is dropped.

rows.value: Features shared across more seeds have higher average explanation scores, but some latents found only in one seed have high scores.
rows.note: The comparison shows that some unmatched features are interpretable; the text does not give numeric group averages here.
rows.check: Shows that orphan latents are often interpretable, i.e. genuine seed-specific features. No group means are given; the 0.72 overall mean score is for all latents.
